text: At each step it outputs one number per vocabulary entry, and a separate rule, the decoder , turns those numbers into the next token.
label: core

text: The same model gives repetitive, bland, creative or broken text depending on that rule alone.
label: core

text: This page is about the rule: searching for the most probable text, sampling from a reshaped distribution, forcing a format, and the inference techniques built on sampling.

text: From logits to a token One forward pass ends in a vector of logits z , one per vocabulary entry: 151,936 for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct , the small open model whose real distributions fill the animations below, and 50,257 for GPT-2 .
label: core

text: The softmax turns them into probabilities, with a temperature T that rescales the logits first: p i = exp(z i / T) / Σ j exp(z j / T) z i logit of token i (only differences between logits matter) T temperature: T = 1 is the model's own distribution, T < 1 sharpens it, T > 1 flattens it towards uniform, T → 0 puts all the mass on the top token A decoder then picks a token, appends it, and runs the model again.
label: core

text: Decoders fall into two families.
label: core

text: Search is deterministic and tries to find a high-probability sequence (greedy, beam search).
label: core

text: Sampling draws at random from a reshaped distribution (temperature, then truncation by top-k, top-p, min-p and others).
label: core
key: draws at random from a reshaped distribution

text: A third layer, constraints , removes tokens that would break a required format before either family chooses.
label: core

text: Deterministic search: greedy and beam Greedy decoding takes the argmax token at every step.
label: core
key: takes the argmax token at every step

text: It is locally optimal and globally poor for open-ended text: repetitive and dull.
label: core

text: It is still fine for short factual answers, and it is effectively what temperature 0 means.
label: core
key: fine only for short factual answers

text: Beam search keeps the B highest-probability partial sequences at every step: each is extended by its best next tokens, all candidates are scored by their total log-probability, and only the top B survive.
label: core

text: It is the standard for machine translation and summarisation, where outputs are short and closed-ended.
label: core

text: For open-ended generation it produces degenerate, repetitive, low-diversity text, because high probability is not the same as human-like ( Holtzman et al., 2019 ), and chat LLMs essentially do not use it.
label: core
key: chat LLMs essentially do not use it

label: core

text: Jerome's Three Men in a Boat (1889).
label: core

label: core
key: every score is the model's own log-probability

text: Before: greedy After: beam search, B = 3 Try: step to 4 in beam mode.
label: core

text: Greedy's choice "was very" is still among the candidates but scores below three other branches, so beam search drops it; greedy can never revisit a choice.
label: core

text: After six tokens the best beam is 6.7 times more probable than greedy's text measured here (exp(−7.54 + 9.44); script recompute.py ).
label: core

text: Finding the more probable text does not make it better.
label: core

text: Run both for 80 tokens on the same prompt measured here : Greedy, 80 tokens Beam search, 4 beams, 80 tokens Sampled, T = 1, top-p 0.95 Both searches fall into a loop the model rates as highly probable; the sample wanders but does not repeat.
label: core

text: This is the paradox Holtzman et al. named: "using likelihood as a decoding objective leads to text that is bland and strangely repetitive", and the per-token probability of natural text is "on average, much lower than text generated by beam search" (§4.3).
label: core

text: On 5,000 WebText continuations with GPT-2 Large (762M) they measured perplexity 12.38 for human text against 1.50 for greedy and 1.48 for beam search with 16 beams, and 73.66% of greedy texts repeating (Table 1, paper ).
label: core

text: The Twelve decoders tab reruns that comparison on GPT-2 small.
label: core
key: reruns that comparison on twelve decoders

text: Correction: temperature 0 is greedy, but greedy is not reproducible on a server Greedy is deterministic for a fixed computation.
label: core
key: Greedy is deterministic for a fixed computation

text: A served model is not a fixed computation: the batch it shares with other requests changes the kernels' reduction order.
label: core

text: Thinking Machines sent the same prompt 1,000 times to Qwen3-235B at temperature 0 and got 80 different completions, diverging at token 103; batch-invariant kernels made all 1,000 identical ( He, September 2025 ; how a server forms and reshapes that batch every step is Batching, KV cache and scheduling in depth ).
label: core

text: Anthropic's migration guide says the same of its API: "temperature = 0 ... never guaranteed identical outputs" ( Opus 5.5 migration guide ).
label: core

text: Stochastic sampling: the standard stack Sampling draws the next token at random, but rarely from the raw distribution: pure sampling at T = 1 lets the long tail of unlikely tokens in, and a few bad draws derail the text (Holtzman et al. measured perplexity 22.73 for pure sampling against 12.38 for human text).
label: core

text: The standard stack reshapes the distribution first, in this order: temperature, then truncation, then renormalise, then sample .
label: core
key: temperature, then truncation, then renormalise, then sample

text: Temperature T : divide the logits by T before the softmax.
label: core

text: T < 1 sharpens (more deterministic; T → 0 approaches greedy); T = 1 is the raw distribution; T > 1 flattens towards uniform (more random, more "creative").
label: core

text: Reasoning models often want T around 0.6 to 1.0 to keep exploring (settings below).
label: core

text: Top-k keeps only the k most probable tokens, renormalises and samples ( Fan et al., 2018 , who used k = 10 for stories).
label: core

text: Its flaw: a fixed k ignores the shape of the distribution.
label: core
key: A fixed k ignores the shape

text: When the distribution is sharp, k lets junk in; when it is flat, k cuts off good options.
label: core
key: on a sharp step it lets junk in

text: Top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p (for example 0.9), renormalises and samples ( Holtzman et al. , Eq.
label: core

text: 2: the smallest V (p) with Σ x∈V(p) P(x) ≥ p).
label: core

text: The set adapts to the distribution; top-p was the long-time default for open-ended generation.
label: core

text: Min-p keeps tokens whose probability is at least p min × P(top token), for example 0.05 to 0.1 of the maximum ( Nguyen et al., ICLR 2025 oral ).
label: core

text: The cut scales with the model's confidence: confident steps become near-greedy, uncertain steps stay diverse.
label: core

text: Its authors report better quality and diversity than top-p especially at high temperature; it is implemented in Hugging Face transformers, vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp, and llama.cpp enables it by default (min-p 0.05, common.h ).
label: core

text: Whether it is better is disputed: see the box below.
label: core

text: The before/after below runs the same real distribution through top-p, the method min-p was proposed to replace, and through min-p.
label: core
key: the method min-p was proposed to replace

label: core

text: Disputed: "min-p beats top-p" The min-p paper reports better quality and diversity on GPQA, GSM8K and AlpacaEval creative writing, and a human preference for min-p.
label: core

text: A re-analysis by Schaeffer, Kazdan and Denisov-Blanch (June 2025) found omitted data and incorrect statistical tests in the human evaluation, found that "min-p did not outperform baselines in quality, diversity, or a trade-off between quality and diversity" once hyperparameter counts were controlled, and noted that the community-adoption figures were removed from the paper as unsubstantiated.
label: core

text: What is not in dispute is the mechanism shown above: at high temperature, min-p's cut follows the top token and top-p's does not.
label: core
key: The mechanism above is not in dispute

text: Our own GPT-2 run in Twelve decoders agrees with the mechanism (at T 1.5, min-p 0.1 stays near human perplexity while top-p 0.95 explodes) but measures likelihood under the same model, not quality as judged by people.
label: core

text: The order is not universal "Temperature, then truncation" is how Hugging Face transformers applies its warpers (temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p, typical) and how vLLM does it (penalties, temperature, min-p, then top-k and top-p; where that sampler runs in the engine's step is on vLLM: inside the default engine ). llama.cpp applies temperature last by default (penalties, DRY, top-n-sigma, top-k, typical, top-p, min-p, XTC, temperature), so its truncation sees the T = 1 distribution and temperature only reshapes the survivors.
label: core

text: With llama.cpp's own defaults (top-k 40, top-p 0.95, min-p 0.05) at T 1.5, the uncertain step keeps 14 tokens with temperature last and 34 with temperature first measured here .
label: core
key: keeps 14 tokens with temperature last and 34

label: core

text: Repetition controls Blunt instruments, needed less as models improved and still useful for small models: Repetition penalty ( CTRL, Keskar et al., 2019 , who found θ ≈ 1.2 a good balance with greedy sampling): every token already in the context has its logit divided by θ if positive and multiplied by θ if negative ( transformers' implementation , which counts the prompt too).
label: core

text: Presence and frequency penalties (the OpenAI-style pair): z j → z j − c j ·α frequency − [c j > 0]·α presence , where c j counts how often token j was already sampled; "around 0.1 to 1" to reduce repetition somewhat, up to 2 to suppress it strongly at a cost in quality ( OpenAI docs ).
label: core

text: Qwen3's model card suggests presence_penalty 0 to 2 against endless repetition, warning of language mixing at high values ( card ).
label: core

text: No-repeat n-gram bans any token that would complete an n-gram already generated (transformers' no_repeat_ngram_size ).
label: core

text: They are blunt because they cannot tell a loop from a correct repeat.
label: core
key: cannot tell a loop from a correct repeat

text: In the lab's "pattern" prompt (continue "red, blue, red, blue, red,") the right answer is a word already in the context; a repetition penalty of 1.3 pushes it down.
label: core

text: What each keeps: Sampler Rule Source Typical sampling Keep the tokens whose surprisal −log p is closest to the distribution's entropy, until their mass reaches typical_p ("entropy-relative") Meister et al., 2022 ; in the lab Mirostat Adjust a top-k-like cut on the fly so that the text's surprise stays near a target (target perplexity, τ = 5 by default in llama.cpp) Basu et al., 2020 Top-a Keep tokens above a threshold proportional to the square of the top probability local-model community; origin unconfirmed XTC (exclude top choices) With some probability, remove every token above a threshold except the least likely of them: cuts the most likely tokens, not the least, to break clichés p-e-w, text-generation-webui PR 6335 (2024) DRY (don't repeat yourself) Penalise a token that would extend a sequence already in the context, by multiplier × base (length − allowed length) (base 1.75, allowed length 2 in llama.cpp) llama.cpp common.h The Sampler lab runs temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p, typical, the repetition penalty and the presence and frequency penalties on 32 real distributions from four prompts, in either order, and samples from the result.
label: depth

text: Diversity against quality Every truncation trades diversity for staying in the model's high-probability region.
label: core

text: The Twelve decoders tab measures the trade on GPT-2 small: four passages, 48 new tokens, 16 samples per decoder measured here .
label: core

text: The pattern reproduces Holtzman et al.'s Table 1 independently, on a smaller model and different text: Greedy and beam search sit far below human perplexity (2.3 and 2.4 against 31.0 for the real continuation) and repeat: 53% of greedy's 4-grams are repeats.
label: core

text: Pure sampling overshoots (47.2); top-p 0.95 at T 1 lands closest to human text (31.6 against 31.0), as nucleus sampling did in the paper (13.13 against 12.38).
label: core

text: Structured, or constrained, decoding A constraint guarantees that the output matches a format (a JSON schema, a regular expression, a context-free grammar) by masking invalid tokens at every step: compile the constraint to an automaton over the tokenizer's vocabulary, intersect it with the current state, and set the disallowed logits to −∞ before the sampler runs.
label: core
key: compiles the constraint to an automaton

text: The animation runs Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on one request, with greedy decoding, without and with a grammar for {"name": string, "age": integer} .
label: core

text: Before: unconstrained After: grammar-constrained The request is illustrative (a made-up person); everything else is the model's real output measured here .
label: core

text: The grammar is a regular expression with whitespace capped at two characters between tokens of JSON, checked against all 151,665 tokenizer entries at every step; a token is allowed when the text so far plus the token can still complete a match.
label: depth

text: A tick marks tokens the grammar allows.
label: core
key: A tick marks tokens the grammar allows

label: core

text: Then step 2 of the constrained run: the model wants two spaces of indentation, the toy grammar's whitespace cap forbids the second, and it is forced onto a token it gave 0.0004%.
label: core

text: The output is still valid JSON, with one-space indentation.
label: core

text: Three engines do this in production: Outlines compiles a regular expression or JSON schema to a finite-state machine over tokens and indexes, for every state, which tokens are allowed: "transitions between the states of a finite-state machine" ( Willard and Louf, 2023 ).
label: core
key: transitions between the states of a finite-state machine

text: It is the approach that popularised near-zero-overhead structured output.
label: core

text: XGrammar handles full context-free grammars with a pushdown automaton.
label: core

text: It splits tokens into context-independent ones, whose validity depends only on the automaton's position and is precomputed, and context-dependent ones, checked at runtime against a persistent stack: for Llama-3.1 and a JSON grammar the context-dependent tokens are "less than 1% (1134 out of 128k)", cut to 120 by context expansion.
label: core

text: It overlaps mask computation with the GPU's forward pass; masks take under 40 µs per token for JSON schema ( Dong et al. ).
label: core

text: It is the default structured-output backend in vLLM (the "auto" backend tries XGrammar first and falls back to llguidance: sampling_params.py ), in SGLang ( serving_hook.py ), TensorRT-LLM and MLC-LLM ( README ). llguidance (behind Guidance) runs an Earley parser on top of a lexer built from regular-expression derivatives and computes masks lazily by walking a trie of the vocabulary, about 50 µs per token for a 128k tokenizer. "LLGuidance shipped in OpenAI for JSON Schema", and it is integrated in llama.cpp, vLLM (from 0.8.2), SGLang (from 0.4.4) and Chromium ( README ).
label: core
key: tries XGrammar first and falls back to llguidance

text: Provider-side "structured outputs" and strict function calling are this mechanism plus training.
label: core

text: OpenAI's launch post: Structured Outputs works "by constraining OpenAI models to match developer-supplied schemas and by training our models to better understand complicated schemas"; the schema is converted to a context-free grammar; gpt-4o-2024-08-06 scored 100% on its complex-schema eval against under 40% for gpt-4-0613 ( OpenAI, 6 August 2024, archived ).
label: core

text: JSON mode guarantees valid JSON; only Structured Outputs guarantees schema adherence ( docs ).
label: core

text: Grammar-constrained tool-call parsing is standard in serving stacks.
label: core

text: Caveats Constraining distorts the distribution.
label: core
key: It guarantees the format, not the content

text: When the model wanted a token you masked, the rest of the answer is conditioned on text it would not have written.
label: core
key: conditioned on text it would not have written

text: Schema design (field order, letting the model think before the JSON) mitigates it.
label: core

text: The size of the effect is disputed: Tam et al., 2024 report "a significant decline in LLMs reasoning abilities under format restrictions"; the Outlines team re-ran their tasks with matched prompts and found structured generation slightly better (GSM8K 0.78 against 0.77, Last Letter 0.77 against 0.73, Shuffled Objects 0.44 against 0.41: .txt, "Say what you mean" ).
label: core

text: Whitespace and token boundaries are the classic bugs.
label: core
key: Whitespace and token boundaries are the classic bugs

text: A token can straddle a grammar boundary ( ": closes a key and starts the colon), whitespace rules decide which tokenisations are reachable (step 2 above), and an unbounded whitespace rule lets a model emit spaces forever.
label: core

text: Techniques built on sampling Self-consistency and best-of-n sample n answers and return the majority answer ( Wang et al., 2022 ) or the one a reward model or verifier rates highest.
label: core

text: Best-of-n is also a baseline alignment method and a reward-hacking amplifier ( Reward Hacking ).
label: core

text: Speculative decoding : a cheap draft model (or n-gram lookup, or extra heads as in Medusa and EAGLE ) proposes γ tokens, and the target model scores all of them in one forward pass.
label: core

text: Each drafted token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), p the target's and q the draft's probability; at the first rejection a replacement is drawn from the normalised max(0, p − q).
label: owned:systems_and_performance/topic_inference_and_serving/speculative_decoding
note: acceptance rule taught on the owner

text: The output distribution is exactly the target's, so the speed-up is lossless ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ).
label: core

text: Common mistakes "Temperature 0 makes the output reproducible" It makes the rule deterministic, not the computation: batching on a shared server changes the numerics (80 distinct completions out of 1,000 in Thinking Machines' test, above). "Top-p 0.9 keeps a handful of tokens" Only at moderate temperature.
label: fat
note: common mistake restating section 1 (80 completions)

text: At T 1.5 on a step where the model is 96% sure, top-p 0.9 keeps 5,166 of 151,936 tokens measured here ; whatever temperature spreads out, top-p collects back. "Min-p is proven better than top-p" The mechanism is real; the evidence that it improves quality is disputed (Schaeffer et al., 2025).
label: fat
note: restates the predict block and section 2

text: Tune both on your own task. "The sampler order is fixed" Hugging Face and vLLM apply temperature before truncation; llama.cpp applies it after by default.
label: fat
note: restates section 2 order

text: The same settings keep different token sets. "Beam search finds better text" It finds more probable text, which for open-ended generation is more repetitive text (the loops above).
label: fat
note: restates section 1

text: Use it for short closed-ended outputs. "A repetition penalty is free" It penalises every repeated token, including the correct ones (a name, a pattern, code identifiers). "Constrained decoding cannot hurt quality" It guarantees the format, not the content: when the grammar overrules the model (0.0004% in the example above) everything after is conditioned on text it would not have written.

text: Measures, all on GPT-2 small: Perplexity : exp of minus the mean log-probability per token at T = 1 (how surprised the model is by the text; human text is the target, not the minimum) Repetition : share of a text's 4-grams that repeat an earlier 4-gram Diversity : distinct-2 over the 16 samples of a passage (greedy and beam give one text 16 times, so their figure is divided by 16) Hover a dot for its decoder; on a narrow screen only a few dots are labelled and the table below has every value.
